title: Intel’s $2.3 Billion Bet on a Quantum Future is a Decade in the Making
gist: Intel is buying Israeli quantum software maker Classiq for $2.3 billion, a deal expected to close in 2H next year. The purchase is meant to turn Intel's 10-year quantum R&D effort into a full-stack commercial business with a modality-neutral software layer. Management warns it will not be high-margin from day one and is happening while Intel is still mid-turnaround and loss-making.

insights.claim: Intel agreed to acquire six-year-old Israeli quantum software company Classiq for $2.3 billion, with closing expected in the second half of next year.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: This is a large quantum software M&A outlay from a chipmaker that is still losing money.
insights.quote: The deal is expected to close in the second half of next year.
insights.locator: Even so, innovation at Intel hasn't stalled

insights.claim: Classiq raised about $200 million over six years, and last year's valuation estimates ran from $400 million to $600 million, so Intel's $2.3 billion price is roughly 4-6x those private-market marks.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: The steep premium points to strategic scarcity pricing for quantum software assets, and it can serve as a comparable for other quantum software valuations.
insights.quote: Classiq has raised some $200 million over multiple investment rounds over its six years, with valuation estimates ranging from $400 million to $600 million last year.
insights.locator: Minerbi claimed Classiq has generated

insights.claim: Classiq has about 130 employees and more than four dozen enterprise customers, including Comcast, AT&T, BMW, Rolls-Royce, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, NTT Data, Mphasis, Lufthansa and Wells Fargo.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: At about $17.7M per employee, Intel is paying mainly for the customer base and the platform, not for headcount.
insights.locator: Classiq has more than four dozen enterprise customers

insights.claim: Classiq's CEO says the company had very healthy revenue this year and expects a very healthy revenue CAGR in the coming years, but gave no figures.
insights.speaker: Nir Minerbi
insights.so_what: Without disclosed revenue, the deal multiple cannot be checked, so treat the growth claims as promotional.
insights.locator: Minerbi claimed Classiq has generated

insights.claim: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan reportedly invested in Classiq about four years before Intel agreed to acquire it.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: This is a potential related-party angle that governance-focused investors may scrutinize.
insights.quote: the company – which Tan reportedly invested in four years ago
insights.locator: Nir Minerbi, Classiq co-founder and chief executive

themes.theme: From R&D lab to quantum business

insights.claim: Intel CTO Pushkar Ranade says Intel's quantum group spent 10 years as a pure R&D project, and the Classiq acquisition is meant to turn it into an actual commercial quantum computing business.
insights.speaker: Pushkar Ranade
insights.so_what: Intel quantum moves from a cost center toward a revenue line, and it could eventually be reported as its own segment.
insights.quote: It moves our quantum computing group from just a research-and-development focus to an actual quantum computing business.
insights.locator: Classiq will turn what has been a lab project

insights.claim: Intel's CTO admitted the company had not really done much customer engagement or commercialization of its quantum technology before the Classiq deal.
insights.speaker: Pushkar Ranade
insights.so_what: Intel is in effect buying a go-to-market channel, and it starts well behind IBM and Google on customer engagement.
insights.quote: really done much by way of customer engagement or trying to commercialize our technology.
insights.locator: Classiq has more than four dozen enterprise customers

insights.claim: Intel's CTO cautioned that quantum will not be a high-margin business from day one and is a long-term bet that Intel must pursue on top of its mainstream businesses.
insights.speaker: Pushkar Ranade
insights.so_what: Expect the deal to dilute margins near term at a company already under cost pressure, with payoff years away.
insights.quote: But this is not going to be a high-margin business from day one. This is really a bet on the future
insights.locator: Despite the enthusiasm of both companies

insights.claim: With Classiq, Intel aims to become a full-stack quantum company that competes with IBM and Google, in a market the article says could grow to as much as $20 billion in the next few years.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Against a $20B market, a $2.3B software purchase is a meaningful claim on the stack.
insights.quote: a market tipped to grow to up to $20 billion in the next few years.
insights.locator: Classiq should allow Intel to become

insights.claim: Intel says it is open to acting as a quantum foundry for discrete parts of the stack, and it also wants to be a quantum system provider that builds whole quantum computers.
insights.speaker: Pushkar Ranade
insights.so_what: This dual foundry-plus-systems strategy mirrors Intel's broader IFS tension and risks channel conflict with quantum hardware rivals who might use its fabs.
insights.quote: We are open to being part of a quantum foundry for discrete components of this stack
insights.locator: Intel also will aggressively pitch its foundry

insights.claim: Classiq's CEO argues the quantum field had real hardware progress but almost no software stack (no OS, no compiler, no development environment), so programming was limited to gate-level work, which he likens to designing a chip at the transistor level.
insights.speaker: Nir Minerbi
insights.so_what: Value may shift toward abstraction layers as hardware matures, which echoes the classical EDA and compiler playbook.
insights.quote: No OS, no compiler, no development environment. Basically, the development was limited to gate-level programming, which is a bit like designing a chip at the transistor level.
insights.locator: There were quite a few players

insights.claim: To make its platform hardware-agnostic, Classiq borrowed classical-computing scaling techniques, including EDA technologies, modeling, synthesis and compilation, and it offers AI natural-language tools and a Python-like language for building quantum algorithms.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: An EDA-style synthesis layer could become the quantum equivalent of the moat Synopsys and Cadence hold in classical chips.
insights.locator: To make the software platform hardware-agnostic

insights.claim: Minerbi argues that every computing revolution so far has been led by capable hardware plus software that unlocked its value, and that Intel already holds the hardware pieces: a silicon QPU, control electronics, foundry services, a simulation stack and the Quantum SDK.
insights.speaker: Nir Minerbi
insights.so_what: This is the logic of vertical integration: software is how hardware gets monetized.
insights.quote: Any computing revolution so far was led by strong hardware, capable hardware, and software that unlocked its value
insights.locator: Any computing revolution so far

insights.claim: Minerbi says the focus of more and more quantum companies is widening beyond hardware and qubits to software, algorithms, architectures, digital twins and networking.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Quantum investment opportunity is spreading beyond qubit makers into the enabling layers.
insights.locator: As development of quantum computers accelerates

insights.claim: Intel has bet its quantum hardware on spin qubits, and the article says Classiq's modality-neutral platform gives Intel a hedge because it remains unclear which modality will win.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Owning the software layer lets Intel capture value even if spin qubits lose to superconducting, neutral-atom, trapped-ion or photonic machines.
insights.quote: It’s unclear which modalities – as the quantum computing field matures – will come to the forefront.
insights.locator: But there are a host of modalities

insights.claim: The article maps the competing quantum modalities to players: superconducting (IBM, Google, D-Wave), neutral atoms (QuEra, Atom Computing, Infleqtion), trapped ions (IonQ, Quantinuum) and photonics (PsiQuantum, Xanadu).
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: This is a handy competitive map: Classiq-under-Intel will sit across all of these vendors' hardware.
insights.locator: But there are a host of modalities

insights.claim: Intel chose spin qubits mainly because they can be manufactured easily on conventional semiconductor equipment, and it builds its QPUs and control chips on 18A logic at its Oregon fab, with 18A-Q and 18A-C variants.
insights.speaker: Pushkar Ranade
insights.so_what: Intel's quantum edge rests on existing fab scale, which ties the bet to 18A process success.
insights.quote: it lends itself very easily to manufacturing on conventional semiconductor equipment.
insights.locator: Intel also will aggressively pitch its foundry

insights.claim: Intel's existing quantum portfolio includes the 12-qubit silicon spin-qubit Tunnel Falls QPU, the Intel Quantum SDK and Horse Ridge control chips developed in 2019.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: At 12 qubits, Intel's hardware is small next to rivals, which explains why it is leaning on software and foundry.
insights.locator: Intel has spent the past decade quietly

insights.claim: Classiq's CEO calls silicon-based spin qubits the most promising modality, while also promising customers that Intel will be ready whatever modality they choose.
insights.speaker: Nir Minerbi
insights.so_what: The seller is talking its book: it backs spin qubits while pitching modality neutrality.
insights.quote: silicon-based – which is the most promising modality
insights.locator: Any computing revolution so far

insights.claim: Intel lost $11 billion in its fiscal 2026 second quarter and is due to report its next quarterly results on October 29, while CEO Lip-Bu Tan cuts costs and scales back earlier expansion plans.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A $2.3B long-dated bet during heavy losses signals management's priorities and adds pressure on capital allocation.
insights.quote: Intel lost $11 billion in its FY 2026 second quarter
insights.locator: Intel’s struggles for much of the past decade

insights.claim: The article argues Intel benefits from AI's shift from training to inference, a more CPU-intensive workload that could narrow the gap between CPUs and GPUs.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A bull case for an Intel CPU recovery is building on inference demand.
insights.quote: a more CPU-intensive workload that could narrow the gap between CPUs and GPUs in the fast-growing AI market.
insights.locator: Intel’s struggles for much of the past decade
